replies.text: [2023/05/30 (Tue) 00:00] I've been trying to improve my photography skills and was wondering if you could give me some tips on how to take better portraits. I've been experimenting with different angles and lighting setups, and I recently got a new 50mm f/1.8 prime lens that I'm still getting used to.
replies.reply:
Nice choice with the 50mm f/1.8 — it's a great learning lens. A few tips:

**Lighting:** Soft, directional light flatters faces best. Try window light at a 45-degree angle to your subject, or shoot outdoors in open shade rather than harsh midday sun. Golden hour (shortly after sunrise or before sunset) is forgiving and warm.

**The lens:** f/1.8 gives beautiful background blur, but at that aperture focus is razor-thin — aim for the eye closest to camera, and consider stopping down to f/2.8–f/4 when shooting couples or groups so no one's face goes soft. Also, 50mm on most crop sensors behaves like ~75–80mm, which is actually flattering for portraits; on full-frame, step back a bit rather than getting too close, since proximity can distort features.

**Angles:** Eye level or slightly above usually works well. Slightly above is slimming; slightly below can be dramatic but risky.

**Beyond gear:** Focus on your subject's comfort — genuine Expression beats perfect lighting. Talk to them, shoot candid moments between poses, and keep the eyes sharp and catching some light (a little "catchlight" brings portraits alive).

What camera body are you pairing the lens with? That'd help me give more specific advice.

replies.text: I'm especially interested in mastering my 50mm lens that I got a month ago. Can you give me some tips on how to best use its shallow depth of field to create a nice bokeh effect?
replies.reply:
Great timing — that f/1.8 aperture is exactly where the bokeh magic happens. A few tips:

**Getting the blur:** Shoot wide open (smallest f-number) and get close to your subject while keeping the background well behind them. Compression and distance between subject and background matter more than people realize — a subject a few meters from the background gives smoother blur than one standing against a wall.

**What's in the background:** Bokeh quality depends on background content. Highlights (streetlights, sun through leaves, fairy lights) turn into pleasing glowing orbs; busy, cluttered scenes just look messy. Seek out good materials.

**Focus discipline:** At f/1.8 the focus plane is razor-thin. Lock onto the eye closest to you — if the eye is sharp, softness elsewhere reads as artistic; if the eye is off, nothing saves the shot. Use single-point AF and confirm before recomposing.

**Know when not to go wide open:** If you're slightly off-angle to the face, or want a bit more of the subject in focus, f/2.2–2.8 often looks better than f/1.8. It also sharpens up the lens considerably.

**One caution:** those cheap "f/1.8" apertures can cause fringing on high-contrast edges wide open — slightly stopped down fixes it.

Do you know which camera body you're pairing it with? On a crop sensor it behaves more like a 75–80mm, which is actually still lovely for portraits.

replies.text: I've been playing around with the lens, trying to get used to the manual focus ring. It's definitely taking some getting used to, but the image quality is so much better than my old kit lens. I took it with me on the coastal trip and got some great portraits of my friends.
replies.reply: Sounds like the trip was the perfect practice run — coastal light plus friends shooting is a great combo for that lens. Manual focus is fiddly at first, but a trick for portraits at f/1.8: focus on the eye closest to camera, and if keepers are coming out soft, nudge to f/2.8 for friends who keep moving. If you want, share what didn't work on the trip and we can troubleshoot from there.

replies.text: The coastal trip was amazing! One of my favorite shots from the trip is a portrait of my friend standing on a cliff overlooking the ocean. I used a fast shutter speed to freeze the motion of the waves and the wind blowing through her hair. The 50mm f/1.8 lens really brought out the details in her face and the background, and the shallow depth of field helped to separate her from the scenery. I'm thinking of printing that one out and framing it for my living room.
replies.reply:
That sounds like a keeper — cliff, ocean, and wind-blown hair is a great recipe for a portrait worth framing. One small thing worth double-checking: a fast shutter freezes motion, but if the waves look solidly sharp too, that's often a wider aperture and good light working together more than the shutter speed. Either way, the result counts.

For the print: since she's a friend, ask her the size you'll want first — a big living room print magnifies any softness in the eye closest to camera. If it's tack-sharp there, go large. Then matte or fine-art paper rather than glossy tends to suit a coastal portrait like that better. Which size are you picturing?

replies.text:
I did have to make some adjustments to my camera settings to account for the bright coastal light. I had to dial down the exposure compensation to avoid blowing out the highlights in the sky, and I also used a polarizing filter to reduce the glare from the water. Additionally, I shot in RAW format to give myself more flexibility during post-processing.

As for printing and framing, I'm thinking of going with a traditional print and frame. I want the image to have a classic, timeless feel to it, and I think a traditional print and frame will help achieve that. I'm considering using a matte finish to reduce glare and add some texture to the image. I've also been looking at some different frame styles, maybe something with a bit of a rustic or coastal vibe to match the theme of the image.

By the way, speaking of post-processing, I've been meaning to learn more about Lightroom and Photoshop. Do you have any tips or resources you could recommend for getting started with those programs
replies.reply:
Those are all solid calls — exposure compensation down, a polarizer for water glare, and RAW will pay off exactly when you're fine-tuning that print file. The matte finish and a rustic or weathered wood frame sound like a great match for a coastal portrait; if you spot a driftwood or whitewashed frame, that could tie the theme together nicely. (Still worth a quick zoom-in on her closest eye before you commit to print size, since matte paper forgives less than people expect at large sizes.)

For Lightroom and Photoshop, here's where I'd start:

**Lightroom first** — it covers 90% of what your photos need:
- Adobe's own free tutorials on YouTube (the "Lightroom in 5 minutes" style ones) are surprisingly good for orientation.
- Search "RAW exposure correction Lightroom" walkthroughs — one session editing one RAW file end-to-end teaches more than hours of tutorials. Your cliff portrait is a perfect practice candidate.
- Learn the histogram, white balance, exposure/shadows/highlights sliders, and masking (the newer AI masks for sky and subject are handy for coastal shots like yours).

**Photoshop later**, and only for what Lightroom can't do:
- Remove distractions (heal brush), composite/blend exposures, and serious retouching. PiXimperfect on YouTube is the gold standard for that, free.

Aaron Nace (Phlearn) bridged both nicely too. One focused project — edit that portrait from start to finish — will get you further than a dozen tutorial binge sessions.

replies.text:
I think the most challenging part of post-processing for me right now is probably color grading and color management. I've been having trouble getting the colors to look consistent across different images, and I'm not sure how to achieve a specific look or mood through color grading. I've been experimenting with different presets and color profiles, but I'm not entirely sure what I'm doing.

I've also been struggling with noise reduction and sharpening. I've been shooting in RAW, but I'm not sure how to effectively reduce noise without losing detail, and I'm worried that over-sharpening will make my images look unnatural.

Do you have any tips or resources for color grading and color management, as well as noise reduction and sharpening?
replies.reply:
Great timing since you're already editing that cliff portrait — it's the perfect practice file for both of these.

**Color management basics:** Consistency starts before grading. Set the same camera profile and white balance approach on every image in a shoot (even just "auto WB as shot" plus one synced profile). In Lightroom, edit one image from a session, then copy/sync those settings across the set — that's how you get consistency without guessing image by image.

**Achieving a specific look:** Instead of presets you apply blindly, try building a look manually once: pick a mood (say, warm and soft for that coastal portrait), then adjust a handful of things deliberately — 白 balance slightly warm, lift the blacks a touch for a faded feel, shift HSL sliders (e.g., pulling aqua toward teal in the ocean), and add a subtle split-tone. Save that as your own preset. You'll learn what each control does far faster, and your presets will actually be yours. Good resources: the Adobe Lightroom tutorials are decent, and for color theory the free "Color Grading 101" content by photographers like Sean Tucker or the YouTuber Mckinnon-style HSL walkthroughs are approachable.

**Noise reduction:** RAW noise is best handled early. Don't crank luminance noise reduction — try Lightroom's newer AI Denoise (it's very good and preserves detail far better than the old manual sliders), around 40–60% for typical high-ISO shots. Also, exposure matters: a slightly underexposed RAW shows more noise, so lift shadows gently rather than fully.

**Sharpening:** The over-sharpening worry is real, but Lightroom's default is conservative. Zoom to 100%, sharpen mainly on detail, keep the masking slider high (hold Alt/Option while dragging to see the mask — only edges should be white, not skin or sky). Sharpen output-dependent: less for large prints since viewing distance is farther.

If you want a concrete exercise: grade and sharpen that cliff portrait using just the HSL panel and the two sliders above, then compare against the original. Want me to walk through one specific look step by step?

replies.text: [2023/05/30 (Tue) 02:19] I'm looking for some tips on editing photos of landscapes. I just got back from a road trip to the coast with friends last week and took some amazing shots of the cliffs and beaches.
replies.reply:
Great trip subject — cliffs and beaches give you so much to work with in post, especially since you shot RAW. A few tips:

**Start with the histogram.** Coastal scenes have extreme brights (sky, water) and darks (shadowed rock faces). Check that the sky isn't clipped and lift shadows on the cliffs gently — past +40 or so shadows start looking muddy.

**Use a graduated filter or mask for the sky.** Dropping the exposure and highlights just on the sky recovers cloud detail without flattening the whole frame. You already dialed exposure down at capture, so you likely have good data to pull back.

**Dehaze, sparingly.** Coastal air flattens distant cliffs; a small dehaze bump (10–20) adds punch and color depth. Push too far and it looks chalky.

**White balance for mood.** Beach shots often benefit from slightly warmer temps (golden sand, sunset glow); if you kept the polarizer on, colors are already cleaner, so nudge rather than overhaul.

**Local edits beat global ones.** Dodge the wet sand line, darken the water for texture, tame a hot highlight on white foam. Same tool set you've been practicing on the cliff portrait — landscapes just reward it more.

**Sharpen for output.** Apply capture sharpening on the RAW file with masking (hold Alt/Option while dragging the masking slider so only edges get sharpened), then adjust final sharpening depending on whether these are destined for screen or print.

Want to pick one of the cliff/beach shots and work through it end to end like you've been doing with the portrait?

replies.text: I've been using Lightroom for most of my editing, and I'm pretty comfortable with it. I'm aiming for a natural look that still brings out the vibrant colors of the coast. Last Sunday, I went to the nearby park and took some photos of the flowers and trees, and I was experimenting with different apertures and shutter speeds to get some nice bokeh effects. But I think the coastal shots from the week before that are more striking - we spent three days driving along the coastal highway, stopping at all the scenic overlooks and taking in the views.
replies.reply:
A park day playing with bokeh is great practice, but I agree the coastal shots will reward the edit more. Since you want natural-but-vibrant, keep a light touch: pull highlights down on the water and sky, lift shadows on the cliffs just enough, then a gentle boost to vibrance rather than saturation — vibrance protects already-bright coastal blues from going cartoonish. A small tightening of whites and blacks adds punch without looking processed, and the polarizer shots should pop with barely any effort.

Pick which cliff or beach shot you want to work through, and let me know if it's headed for screen or print — the print one matters most for how far you can push vibrance.

replies.text: One of my favorites is a shot of a seagull flying overhead, its wings spread wide. I used a fast shutter speed to freeze the motion, and it turned out really well.
replies.reply:
A frozen seagull with wings spread is a great complement to the cliff portrait you mentioned as your favorite — birds are one of the few subjects where a fast shutter really is doing the heavy lifting, so nice instinct there. For editing, that shot will love the same natural-but-vibrant treatment: watch the highlights on the white feathers, since gulls clip easily against a bright sky, and a touch of texture or clarity on the wings can bring out the feather detail.

So now you've got two strong contenders from the trip — the portrait and this seagull — plus the broader cliff/beach shots. Which one are we walking through first in Lightroom, and is it headed for screen or print?

replies.text: I've been thinking about printing that one out and framing it for my living room. I think it would make a great addition to my decor.
replies.reply:
The cliff portrait already feels like a print piece, and your maternal instinct is right — that driftwood-style frame would make it a real focal point rather than just a photo on a wall. I'd say go for it.

One practical note before you commit to a size: zoom way in on her closest eye on your monitor at 100%. At f/1.8 the depth of field is razor-thin, and a print at living-room size magnifies any softness that's invisible on a phone screen. If the eye is tack-sharp, you can confidently go large. And since you're editing in Lightroom anyway, once you've done the natural-but-vibrant pass, export it with print-specific sharpening — paper softens a print slightly compared to a screen, especially matte.

Want to do the Lightroom walk-through on this one next, so the file's ready whenever the print shop trip happens?

replies.text: I've heard good things about online printing services like Shutterfly or Snapfish, but I've also considered using a local print shop to get it done. I think I'll do some research and compare prices and quality before making a decision.
replies.reply: Smart move comparing before committing. For your cliff portrait specifically, a local shop has two real advantages: you can view physical paper sample swatches next to your file, and soft-proofing on a calibrated local printer matters more at large sizes. Shutterfly-style services are cheaper and convenient, but one-off fine-art quality is usually better at a dedicated print lab — and if you do go online, I'd look at a photo-focused lab rather than a general consumer service. Either way, ask for matte/fine-art paper to match your plan.

replies.text: I'm open to suggestions. I've heard that matte papers are good for reducing glare, but I'm not sure if that's the best option for my image. What do you think?
replies.reply:
Honestly, for this specific image, I'd stick with matte — and I think you already sensed why. Your cliff portrait has blown-sky risk baked into the scene, soft shallow depth of field, and a coastal theme that suits a natural, low-glare finish. Matte/fine-art paper handles that classic, timeless look better, and you've been leaning that way all along.

A couple of refinements to consider:

- **Look at "lustre" too.** It's between matte and glossy — most of matte's glare resistance with slightly richer color and better shadow depth. It's often the sweet spot for portraits and worth comparing with a physical sample.
- **What matters more than surface is the paper body.** A heavier cotton/fine-art matte paper will flatter that 50mm f/1.8 detail far more than a cheap glossy would.
- Ask whichever printer you visit (or order from) for a soft proof or small test strip before committing to the large living-room size.

So: yes, matte is the right call for this image — just make it a good matte, and check lustre samples if you get the chance.
